stories.title: The Stone That Fell from the Sky

pages.text: For most of his fifteen years, Fahad had thought of the Empty Quarter as nothing more than a huge blank space on the map of Arabia. So when his Uncle Majed, a geologist, invited him on a three-day expedition to the Wabar craters, he could hardly believe his luck. According to his uncle, a meteorite had crashed into the sand there hundreds of years ago, scattering fragments of iron across the dunes. "If we're lucky, we might find a piece that nobody has touched since it fell," Uncle Majed said, his eyes shining. Fahad packed his bag that night, although he was far too excited to sleep.

They set off before dawn, the four-wheel-drive car humming along a rough track until even the track gave up and disappeared. All around them, dunes rose like frozen waves, shifting from pale gold to deep orange as the sun climbed higher. Uncle Majed explained that the impact had been so violent that it had melted the sand into black glass, which local people had once called "desert pearls." Fahad listened, but part of his mind drifted back to his grandfather, who had spent his youth crossing these sands with camels. "The desert takes away every road," the old man liked to say, "but it can never take away the stars."

By midday they had reached the craters, wide hollows half buried by centuries of drifting sand. They spent hours walking slowly across the ground, heads bent, examining every dark shape they came across. Fahad picked up a heavy, rust-coloured stone and held it out hopefully, but his uncle only glanced at it and shrugged. "Probably just an ordinary rock, but keep it if you like," he said kindly. Fahad slipped it into his pocket anyway, feeling a little foolish. Then, late in the afternoon, he noticed that the horizon had turned a strange, dirty yellow.

"Sandstorm," Uncle Majed muttered. "Get in the car, quickly!" Within minutes the wind was howling like an angry animal, and the world outside the windows vanished into a whirling cloud of dust. They sat in silence for nearly two hours while sand hissed against the metal and the car rocked from side to side. When the storm finally died down, the landscape looked completely unfamiliar, and their tyre tracks had been wiped away as if they had never existed. Worse still, the GPS screen had gone blank, and the satellite phone, which had been charging from the faulty socket, was completely dead.

As if things weren't bad enough, Uncle Majed twisted his ankle while climbing a dune to look around. He limped back to the car, his face tight with pain, and admitted that the wheels had sunk deep into the soft sand. "We should have been more careful," he sighed. "Nobody is expecting us back for two more days." Fahad felt panic rising in his chest, but he forced himself to breathe slowly. If they waited for rescue, they might run out of water; if they drove in the wrong direction, they could end up even more lost.

That was when Fahad remembered the patrol road his uncle had pointed out on the paper map, running roughly north of the craters. "If I can find north, we can find the road," he said, surprising himself with how calm he sounded. First, following his uncle's instructions, he let some air out of the tyres and dug the sand away from the wheels until his hands were raw. Because his uncle's left ankle was injured and the car was automatic, Uncle Majed could still drive with his right foot. Then, as darkness fell and the sky filled with countless stars, Fahad searched for the shape his grandfather had taught him to recognise. There it was: the faint, steady light of the North Star, which never moves while the other stars turn around it.

They drove at a snail's pace through the night, with Fahad leaning out of the window to keep the star directly ahead of them. Every few minutes doubt crept in, and he wondered whether he had made a terrible mistake. "Are you sure about this?" he asked once, his voice shaking slightly. "I trust you more than I trust that broken screen," his uncle replied, and the words gave Fahad the courage to keep going. Hours passed, and the stars wheeled slowly overhead, but the North Star held its position, just as his grandfather had promised.

Just as the sky began to lighten before dawn, the car's headlights caught something straight and solid among the dunes. It was the patrol road, exactly where Fahad had hoped it would be. They stopped to pray, and soon afterwards a Bedouin herder appeared with his camels, as if the desert itself had sent him. He welcomed them warmly, offering sweet tea and dates, and used his own phone to call for help. When Fahad explained how they had found the road, the old herder nodded with approval. "Your grandfather taught you well," he said. "Few young people today can read the sky."

A week later, back in Riyadh, Uncle Majed phoned with news that left Fahad speechless. Almost as an afterthought, he had taken the rust-coloured stone to the university laboratory, and the tests had revealed that it was genuine meteoritic iron. "It seems I owe you an apology, and probably a place in my next research paper," his uncle laughed. That evening, Fahad placed the stone in his grandfather's wrinkled hand and told him the whole story. The old man turned it over slowly, then smiled. "So the sky gave you two gifts," he said, "a stone to hold, and the stars to guide you home."

pages.text: It was 11:47 on a Thursday night when Faisal made the biggest mistake of his fifteen years. He had been chatting with his best friend, Majed, about the family gathering at his grandparents' house the next day. "Honestly," he said into his phone, holding down the record button, "if Aunt Huda brings that date cake again, I'm going to fake an illness. Last time I nearly broke a tooth, and I'm telling you, it's not a cake, it's a building material." He let go of the button, sent the message, and only then noticed the name at the top of the screen: "The Family 🌴 (43 members)".

For three long seconds, Faisal simply stared, unable to breathe. Then he jabbed at the screen, desperate to delete the message for everyone. At that exact moment, his phone, which he had been meaning to charge for two hours, gave a tiny, sad buzz and went completely black. By the time he had found his charger under a pile of school books and switched the phone back on, the app kept freezing, and the delete option had mysteriously vanished. Nobody had listened to the message yet, but in a few hours forty-three people would wake up.

In a panic, he woke his older sister, Noura, who listened to his explanation with her eyes half-closed. "So let me get this straight," she said slowly. "You called Aunt Huda's cake a building material, in front of the entire family, including Aunt Huda." "In front of their phones," Faisal corrected her. "That's completely different, because if I can stop them from playing it, nobody ever has to know." Noura yawned and told him that the whole plan was a recipe for disaster, which, under the circumstances, was an unfortunate choice of words.

Fortunately, Faisal's relatives were famous for two things: arriving late and ignoring the family group, except to send pictures of roses every Friday morning. If he got to his grandparents' house early enough, he might be able to intercept every phone before anyone pressed play. He called it Operation Silent Phone, and he spent the rest of the night planning it as carefully as a bank robbery. By the time the sun came up, he had drawn a map of the house, made a list of every relative, and barely slept at all.

At first, the operation went better than he could have dreamed. He offered to update Uncle Saad's phone "for security reasons" and quietly hid the family chat in a folder his uncle would never find. He convinced his twin cousins that Grandfather wanted a phone-free gathering, and they handed over their phones without a single question. Grandmother, whose phone always rang at full volume, happily let him take hers to the kitchen to charge, where it ended up, for reasons he couldn't fully explain, inside an empty rice container. By lunchtime, Faisal was feeling like a secret agent who deserved a medal.

Then, just as everyone was sitting down with their tea, Grandfather cleared his throat and made an announcement. "I have learned something new," he said proudly, holding up his ancient phone, which nobody had even remembered he owned. "Little Abdullah taught me how to listen to these voice messages, so let us hear what the family has been saying." Faisal leapt forward, but he tripped over a cushion, and before he could get up, Grandfather had pressed the newest message with the speaker turned all the way up.

Faisal's voice filled the room, loud and clear: "It's not a cake, it's a building material." The silence that followed was the longest of his life, and he would have given anything for the floor to swallow him whole. Aunt Huda slowly put down her cup, and every head turned towards her, then towards Faisal, who was still lying on the carpet next to the cushion. Somewhere in the kitchen, as if to make things worse, Grandmother's phone began ringing loudly from inside the rice container.

Then, to everyone's astonishment, Aunt Huda burst out laughing so hard that tears ran down her face. "Twelve years!" she cried. "For twelve years I have baked that awful cake because your grandmother said it was everybody's favourite, and every single one of you kept telling me it was delicious!" One by one, the relatives confessed: Uncle Saad admitted he had been hiding his piece in a napkin, and Grandfather admitted he had been feeding his to the birds in the garden. Even Grandmother, who had suggested the recipe in the first place, confessed that she had never actually tasted it.

"Well," said Aunt Huda, wiping her eyes, "since our young expert has such strong opinions, next Friday he can do the baking." A week later, Faisal proudly carried in his own cake, which had collapsed in the middle and burned around the edges. The family ate it politely, without saying a word, until Faisal's phone buzzed with a new voice note in the family group. It was from Aunt Huda, and it said: "Honestly, it's not a cake, it's a pancake that has given up on life." This time, Faisal laughed louder than anyone.

pages.text: Yousef had spent every afternoon that summer at the marine research station on the Farasan Islands, where his uncle Khalid worked as a biologist. His favourite job was watching a small green dot on a computer screen. The dot was Noor, a young hawksbill turtle who had been fitted with a satellite transmitter three weeks earlier. Every six hours, the dot jumped to a new place as Noor wandered between the reefs of the Red Sea. But on Thursday morning, when Yousef refreshed the map, the dot had not moved at all.

"It's probably just a technical fault," Uncle Khalid said, although he was frowning at the screen. "Transmitters fail more often than people realise." Yousef wasn't convinced, and he could tell his uncle wasn't either. If a turtle stays in one spot for too long, it might be resting, but it might also be trapped. The last signal had come from a reef twelve kilometres north, and by now Noor could be anywhere.

Their grandfather, who had been a fisherman for over forty years, was drinking tea by the window and had overheard everything. "The sea doesn't keep things where you leave them," he said calmly. "The wind has been blowing from the north-west for two days, so the current will have pushed anything floating towards the shallows near the Two Sisters." Uncle Khalid explained that the station's boat was being repaired and wouldn't be ready until the following week. Grandfather simply stood up and reached for his keys. "Then we'll take mine," he said, as if the matter had already been decided.

Grandfather's boat was old and noisy, but it cut through the water with surprising confidence. As they headed north, Yousef began to feel that they were looking for a needle in a haystack, because the sea seemed endless and every wave looked the same. Grandfather, however, kept pointing out details that Yousef would never have noticed: a line of foam where two currents met, a change in the colour of the water, a group of seabirds circling low. "The sea talks all the time," he said. "Most people just haven't learned to listen."

They had been searching for almost two hours when Yousef spotted something dark moving near the surface. As they came closer, his stomach turned. A huge abandoned fishing net, heavy with seaweed and plastic, had drifted into the shallows, and caught inside it was a turtle. One of her front flippers was tightly wrapped in the green ropes, and she was struggling to lift her head to breathe. On her shell, Yousef could just make out the small white device that his uncle had attached.

"We're racing against the clock," Uncle Khalid said, pulling on his mask. "She's exhausted, and if she can't reach the surface, she'll drown." Yousef put on his life jacket and slid into the warm water beside him, while Grandfather held the boat steady against the rising waves. Every time the knife came near, Noor panicked and twisted, pulling the ropes even tighter. Yousef held her shell as gently as he could and spoke to her quietly, although he knew she couldn't understand a word.

At last, the final rope snapped and the net fell away into the blue. Noor floated free, but her flipper was badly cut and she barely moved. "If we release her now, she might not survive," Uncle Khalid said, breathing hard. Together, the three of them lifted her carefully into the boat and wrapped her in a wet towel to keep her cool. Then they did something just as important: they hauled the rest of the net on board so that it could never trap another animal.

Back at the station, the vet examined Noor and said that, with a few weeks of rest, she would recover completely. The transmitter, it turned out, had been crushed by the ropes, which explained why the dot had frozen on the screen. "So the technology told us something was wrong," Yousef said slowly, "but it couldn't tell us where to look." Uncle Khalid smiled and glanced at Grandfather. "Satellites are useful," he admitted, "but they've never spent forty years on the water."

Three weeks later, the whole family gathered on the beach at sunrise to watch Noor return to the sea with a brand-new transmitter. She paused at the edge of the water for a moment, then disappeared beneath the waves without looking back. That evening, a fresh green dot appeared on the screen, moving steadily south. Yousef, meanwhile, had started a new project: a notebook filled with everything his grandfather knew about winds, currents and birds. "One day," he said, "someone will need this knowledge, and I don't want it to be lost."

pages.text: Nora had never thought of herself as an adventurer, so when her father announced that the family would be spending the winter holiday in Uzbekistan, she simply shrugged. That changed the night before they left, when her grandmother called her into her room and placed a faded envelope and half of an old silver coin in her hands. "In 1958, your great-grandfather Abdullah fell seriously ill in Bukhara on his way home from a trading journey," she explained quietly. "A family there looked after him for weeks, and before he left, he broke this coin in two and gave them the other half." She held Nora's gaze. "He always dreamed that someone from our family would go back and thank them properly, and I think that someone should be you."

Two days later, the high-speed train was racing across the frozen plains between Tashkent and Bukhara, while Nora studied the envelope for the hundredth time. The address had been written in an elegant but old-fashioned hand, and according to her phone, half the street names in the city had been changed since then. "Let's be realistic," said her older brother Saud, without looking up from his game. "You're looking for a family you've never met, at an address that probably doesn't exist, from a story that's nearly seventy years old." He grinned. "It's like searching for a needle in a haystack, except someone has moved the haystack."

Unfortunately, Saud turned out to be partly right. When they finally found the spot where the house should have stood, they discovered a smart modern hotel with glass doors and a doorman in a long coat. Nora felt her heart sink, and for a moment she could hardly bring herself to speak. "We've done our best, habibti," her father said gently, resting a hand on her shoulder. "Perhaps we should just enjoy the rest of our trip." However, Nora had made a promise, and she was determined not to give up at the first obstacle.

On the spur of the moment, she marched into the hotel and showed the receptionist a photo of the envelope. The young man frowned at the name for a long time before admitting that he had never heard of the family. "But if anyone knows the history of this city, it's Madina Opa," he added, brightening. "She runs the old bookshop near the Lyabi-Hauz pond, and people say she remembers every story that has ever been told in Bukhara." Nora thanked him so many times that he began to laugh.

The bookshop was tiny and smelled of dust, paper and cardamom tea, and Madina Opa was even tinier, peering at them over a pair of enormous reading glasses. As she examined the envelope, her expression slowly shifted from polite curiosity to astonishment. "My father used to tell this story when I was a girl," she murmured. "A traveller from Arabia who nearly died of fever, and a family of coppersmiths who refused to let him go until he was strong again." She pointed a thin finger towards the window. "If they are still anywhere, they will be in the coppersmiths' quarter, beneath the old trading domes."

By the time Nora and her mother reached the trading domes, the winter sun was already sinking and the air was ringing with the sound of hammers on metal. They went from workshop to workshop, asking the same question again and again, but each craftsman only shook his head apologetically. One by one, the shutters began to come down, and the narrow lanes grew colder and quieter. Nora could feel her hopes fading with the light, and she was beginning to wonder whether she had been foolish to come so far for a story. "One more," her mother insisted, squeezing her hand. "Just one more, and then we'll go."

The last workshop belonged to an elderly man with a white beard, who was polishing a copper tray so carefully that he barely noticed them enter. Nora began to explain, but then she realised he wasn't listening to her words at all; his eyes were fixed on the half-coin in her open palm. Without a word, he put down his cloth and disappeared into the back of the shop. They could hear drawers being opened and boxes being moved, and Nora held her breath. When the old man returned, his hands were trembling, and he was carrying a small wooden box decorated with faded blue paint.

Inside the box, wrapped in a piece of embroidered silk, lay the other half of the coin. When Nora placed the two pieces side by side, they fitted together perfectly, as if they had never been apart. The old man, whose name was Rustam, explained through his grandson that his own grandfather had kept the coin all his life. "He made me promise that I would never sell it, however difficult things became," Rustam said, his voice thick with emotion. "He always said, 'One day, they will come back, and we must be ready to welcome them as family.'" Nora's mother read the letter aloud, translating each line, and by the end, nobody in the workshop had dry eyes.

That evening, Rustam's family insisted on inviting them home for a feast of steaming plov, fresh bread and endless cups of green tea. Nora video-called her grandmother, who wept with joy as Rustam held up his half of the coin to the screen. Before they left, the two families made a decision: rather than joining the coin together, each would keep its half, so that one day another generation would have a reason to make the journey. On the train home, Saud admitted that he had been completely wrong about the haystack. Nora simply smiled and looked out at the snowy plains, realising that the best journeys aren't about the places you see, but about the people who are waiting at the end of them.

This brings me to my next point, which is how we raised the money.

about it
for

Turning now to the results, I'd like to show you what we achieved.

This brings me to my next point, which it is the budget.
This brings me to my next point, what is the budget.
This brings me to my next point, which is the budget.

3-2.answer: It's customary to serve dates with Arabic coffee when guests arrive.
Unlike in many Western countries, people here tend to break their fast with extended family.

options: for
of
to

3-2.q: Your online peer asks: "Why do people shake their coffee cup?" Choose the best reply.
options: Because they want to.
Shaking cup is tradition, yes.
It's customary to gently shake the cup when you've had enough; it tells the host you're finished.
Unlike in the UK, people here tend to visit relatives every weekend.
Unlike in the UK, people here tend to visiting relatives every weekend.
Unlike in the UK, people here tends to visit relatives every weekend.

3-3.answer: I'd been hiking for two hours when suddenly the path disappeared.
No sooner had we arrived at the camp than the sandstorm began.

He pointed out that people used to walk everywhere in the old days.

3-4.q: Apparently, back then, people ___ sleep on the roof during the hot summer nights.
options: will

3-4.q: Your grandfather said: "We didn't have air conditioning." How do you report this?
options: He told me that we don't have air conditioning.

She said me that Riyadh had grown enormously.
She told that Riyadh had grown enormously.

To put it another way, the project depends on young volunteers.

3-5.q: Someone asks: "How much did the restoration cost?" You don't know. Choose the best reply.
options: I'm afraid I don't have the exact figures, but I know it was a major government investment.
That's not important.
I don't know. Next question.
you are wrong about it.
let me think about it for a second.
I not know the answer.
I afraid I don't have the exact figures.
I'm afraid I haven't the exactly figures.

words.ar: يُؤتمت؛ يجعل العمل يتم آليًا دون تدخل بشري
words.ex: Many banks have automated simple tasks like checking account balances.
AI tools can boost productivity by doing repetitive work in seconds.
Over-reliance on chatbots might stop students from thinking for themselves.

words.ar: التعلّم المُخصَّص حسب احتياجات كل طالب
words.ex: Personalised learning apps adjust the difficulty of each exercise to your level.
The main drawback of smart assistants is that they are always listening.
Teachers are worried about the misuse of AI to write homework essays.

dialogue.t: Have you noticed how many of our classmates use AI to help with their homework now?
Definitely. There's no denying that it saves time, yet I think some people are becoming too dependent on it.
I agree. It could easily be used to cheat on essays without the teacher noticing.
True, but it can also explain difficult maths problems step by step, which is really helpful.
What about jobs, though? My uncle says customer service is likely to be replaced by chatbots within a few years.
Some jobs might disappear, but new ones will be created too, like people who design and check these systems.
So overall, do you think the change is positive?
Mostly, as long as we use it to learn rather than to avoid learning.

grammar.title: Passive with modals and 'be likely to'
grammar.ar: نستخدم المبني للمجهول بعد الأفعال الناقصة مثل could و might و will بالصيغة: الفعل الناقص + be + التصريف الثالث، مثل could be used. ونستخدم be likely to be + التصريف الثالث للتعبير عن احتمال كبير بأن يحدث شيء للفاعل دون ذكر من يقوم به. انتبه: لا نحذف be، فلا نقول could used.
examples: Many factory jobs are likely to be replaced by robots in the next decade.
This app could easily be used to translate entire conversations in real time.
Students' data might be shared with other companies without their knowledge.

words.ar: الجاذبية الصغرى؛ حالة انعدام الوزن تقريبًا
words.ex: Scientists study how cells behave in microgravity on the space station.
Rayyanah Barnawi's mission was a historic milestone for Saudi women.
The crew spent about ten days carrying out experiments on the ISS.
Millions of people watched the launch live from Florida.
Some people believe that medical discoveries justify the cost of space missions.
Research in space could lead to a breakthrough in cancer treatment.

dialogue.t: Did you know that Prince Sultan bin Salman was the first Arab in space, back in 1985?
Yes, and he is widely considered to be a pioneer for the whole region.
And in 2023, Rayyanah Barnawi and Ali AlQarni flew to the International Space Station.
Rayyanah is said to have carried out stem cell experiments related to cancer research while she was up there.
That's impressive. But it's been argued that the money would be better spent on problems here on Earth.
I see that point, but many technologies we use daily, like GPS, came from space research.
That's true. And these missions inspire young people to study science.
Exactly. For me, that inspiration alone helps justify the cost.

grammar.title: Reporting with impersonal passives
grammar.ar: نستخدم تراكيب مثل It's been argued that و is said to و is considered to be لنقل آراء أو معلومات عامة دون تحديد قائلها، وهذا شائع في الأخبار والكتابة الرسمية. إذا كان الحدث في الماضي نستخدم to have + التصريف الثالث، مثل is said to have carried out. أما إذا كان الوصف في الحاضر فنستخدم to + المصدر أو to be.
examples: It's been argued that space exploration is a waste of public money.
Ali AlQarni is said to have studied how clouds form while orbiting Earth.
The James Webb telescope is widely considered to be one of the greatest scientific tools ever built.

words.ex: Solar panels on the roof can provide enough electricity for a whole house.
The panels convert sunlight directly into electricity.
Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest producers of water through seawater desalination.
Special membranes filter out salt and other particles from the water.
The water is treated again to remove any remaining impurities.
Extra electricity from the solar farm is sent to the national grid.

dialogue.t: My little brother asked me where our tap water comes from, and I didn't know how to explain desalination simply.
Put simply, desalination works by removing the salt from seawater so we can drink it.
OK, but how exactly is the salt removed?
First, seawater is pumped from the sea and cleaned to remove sand and larger particles.
And after that?
Once the water has been cleaned, it is then pushed at high pressure through very fine membranes that filter out the salt.
So only fresh water gets through?
Exactly. This, in turn, results in clean water that is sent to homes after a final treatment.

grammar.title: Describing processes with the passive
grammar.ar: عند شرح عملية علمية أو صناعية نستخدم المبني للمجهول لأن التركيز يكون على ما يحدث للشيء وليس على من يقوم بالعمل. نستخدم Once + المضارع التام المبني للمجهول (has been + التصريف الثالث) لبيان أن خطوة اكتملت قبل الخطوة التالية. وتساعد عبارات مثل This, in turn, results in و Put simply على ربط الخطوات وتبسيط الشرح.
examples: Once the sunlight has been absorbed by the panels, it is then converted into electricity.
This, in turn, results in lower electricity bills for families.
Put simply, a solar panel works by turning light energy into electrical energy.

words.ex: Driverless taxis could become common in big cities soon.
NEOM is building new infrastructure from scratch, including roads and energy systems.

words.ar: مستدام؛ لا يضرّ بالبيئة على المدى الطويل
words.ex: Future cities will need to be more sustainable to reduce pollution.

words.ar: التنقّل اليومي بين البيت والعمل أو المدرسة
words.ex: A high-speed train could cut my daily commute to just ten minutes.
By 2040, most of our electricity may come from renewable energy.
Virtual reality could transform the way history is taught in schools.

dialogue.t: What do you think cities will look like in 2040?
By 2040, we'll have built cities like NEOM that run completely on renewable energy.
That sounds amazing. What about transport?
In twenty years' time, people will be travelling in driverless cars and high-speed trains instead of driving themselves.
And schools? Will students still sit in classrooms?
Probably, but they'll be using virtual reality to visit places they're studying.
I'm not so sure about one thing, though. I doubt whether robots will ever fully replace teachers.
I agree. Students will always need a real person to motivate them.

grammar.title: Future perfect and future continuous
grammar.ar: نستخدم المستقبل التام (will have + التصريف الثالث) للحديث عن شيء سيكون قد اكتمل قبل وقت محدد في المستقبل، وغالبًا مع By. ونستخدم المستقبل المستمر (will be + فعل -ing) لوصف نشاط سيكون جاريًا في وقت معين في المستقبل. ونعبّر عن الشك في حدوث شيء بعبارة I doubt whether ... will ever.
examples: By 2040, scientists will have found new ways to store solar energy.
In twenty years' time, people will be ordering almost everything by drone delivery.
I doubt whether flying cars will ever be cheap enough for ordinary families.

words.ex: The app's algorithm decides which videos appear on your feed.
Many apps collect personal data such as your location and contacts.
Cyberbullying can be even more harmful because it follows you everywhere.
Endless scrolling is designed to be addictive.

words.ar: غرفة الصدى؛ بيئة لا يرى فيها المستخدم إلا الآراء التي تشبه رأيه
words.ex: Social media can trap teenagers in an echo chamber where they never hear other opinions.
Stronger regulation could protect young users from harmful content.

dialogue.t: Do you ever worry about how much social media apps know about you?
All the time. What worries me most is how they collect our personal data without us really understanding it.
For me, it's the algorithms that really need to be addressed. They keep showing us the same kind of content.
True, and that can be addictive. I sometimes scroll for hours without noticing.
So what's the solution? Should apps be banned for teenagers?
I don't think banning works. The real question is whether companies will take responsibility for protecting young users.
Maybe schools could also teach digital safety, like how to check privacy settings and report cyberbullying.
That's a great idea. Responsibility should be shared by companies, schools and families.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences for emphasis
grammar.ar: الجمل المشقوقة (Cleft sentences) تُستخدم لتسليط الضوء على فكرة معيّنة وإبرازها. نستخدم What + جملة + is لتقديم الفكرة الأهم، مثل What worries me most is... ونستخدم It is/It's + الفكرة المؤكَّدة + that/who لإبراز جزء واحد من الجملة. هذه التراكيب تجعل كلامك أقوى وأكثر إقناعًا في النقاش.
examples: What worries me most is that young children can easily see violent content.
It's the lack of age checks that really needs to be addressed.
The real question is whether teenagers can control their own screen time.

words.ex: My laptop freezes every time I open more than three tabs.
The computer overheats after about an hour of use.
Since the laptop is still under warranty, the repair should be free.
The technician helped me troubleshoot the problem over the phone.
If they can't fix it, I'd like a replacement.
It turned out the battery was faulty from the start.

dialogue.t: Good afternoon, you're through to technical support. How can I help you today?
Hi, I bought a laptop from you two months ago, and it keeps shutting down whenever I start a video call.
I'm sorry to hear that. Have you tried any troubleshooting steps yet?
Yes, I've already tried updating the software and resetting it, but it still won't stay on for more than ten minutes.
It sounds like it might be overheating. We can send a technician to look at it next week.
I really need it for my online classes. Would it be possible to get a replacement instead of waiting for a repair?
Since it's still under warranty, I can arrange a replacement. It should arrive within three working days.
That would be perfect. Thank you for your help.

grammar.title: Describing repeated problems: keep + -ing and won't
grammar.ar: نستخدم keep + فعل -ing لوصف مشكلة تتكرر باستمرار وتسبب الإزعاج، مثل It keeps crashing. ونستخدم still won't + المصدر للتعبير عن أن الجهاز يرفض العمل رغم المحاولات، حيث تعني won't هنا "يرفض" وليس المستقبل. ولطلب حلّ بديل بأدب نستخدم Would it be possible to ... instead of + فعل -ing؟
examples: The screen keeps flickering whenever I open a game.
I've already tried charging it overnight, but it still won't turn on.
Would it be possible to get a refund instead of sending it for repair?

words.ex: I'm really into photography, especially taking pictures of old buildings.

words.ar: يكون متحمسًا لشيء أو راغبًا فيه
words.ex: My brother has never been particularly keen on team sports.
I took up chess last year after watching a tournament online.

words.ar: يسعى إلى بناء مسيرة مهنية في مجال ما
words.ex: She hopes to pursue a career in medicine once she finishes school.
Travelling abroad would really broaden my horizons.
To be honest, I find maths quite challenging, but I enjoy it.

dialogue.t: So, Omar, what do you enjoy doing in your free time?
Well, I'm really into graphic design, which is partly why I spend so much time on my laptop. I've been designing logos for friends for about two years now.
That sounds interesting. And what about sport? Do you play any?
To be honest, I've never been particularly keen on competitive sports, but I do go swimming twice a week because it helps me relax after school.
Which subject do you enjoy most at school?
Probably art, because it gives me the freedom to experiment. Our teacher also encourages us to try digital tools, which I find really motivating.
And what are your plans for the future?
Ideally, I'd like to study design at university once I finish secondary school. Eventually, I'd love to work for an international company and broaden my horizons.

grammar.title: 'Which' referring to a whole idea
grammar.ar: نستخدم which بعد فاصلة لنشير إلى الجملة السابقة كلها وليس إلى اسم واحد فقط، وهذا يساعد على إطالة الإجابة بشكل طبيعي. لاحظ أننا لا نستخدم that في هذه الحالة، ولا نكرر الضمير بعد which كما نفعل أحيانًا في العربية (لا نقول: which it is). هذه البنية تجعل إجاباتك في الامتحان أكثر تطورًا وترابطًا.
examples: I'm really into music, which is partly why I joined the school band.
My parents both work in science, which probably explains my interest in chemistry.
I live close to the sea, which means I can go diving most weekends.

words.ex: Whereas some students prefer studying alone, others work better in groups.
The setting in the second photo looks much more relaxed.
Hands-on activities help students remember what they learn.
Both pictures have teamwork in common.
Phones can be a huge distraction during lessons.
There seems to be a very friendly atmosphere in the workshop.

dialogue.t: Here are your two photographs. They show people learning in different places. Compare them and say what the advantages of each place might be.
OK. Whereas the first photo shows a group of teenagers in a traditional classroom, the second one shows a young man learning to cook in a busy restaurant kitchen.
Both pictures have a teacher figure in common, but the way they're teaching is completely different. In the classroom, the teacher is standing at the front explaining something on the board.
One major difference is that the kitchen is much more hands-on. The young man is actually practising with real ingredients, so he's probably learning by making mistakes.
The classroom might be better for learning theory, because there are fewer distractions. On the other hand, the atmosphere in the kitchen seems more dynamic and realistic.
Thank you. Layla, which place would you prefer to learn in?
Personally, I'd go for the kitchen, because I learn faster when I'm doing something rather than just listening.

grammar.title: Linking contrasts: whereas, while, unlike
grammar.ar: نستخدم whereas و while لربط جملتين كاملتين متناقضتين، ويمكن وضعهما في بداية الجملة أو في وسطها. أما unlike فيأتي بعدها اسم أو ضمير وليس جملة كاملة. تجنّب استخدام but في كل مرة، فتنويع أدوات الربط يرفع درجتك في الامتحان.
examples: Whereas the first photo is taken indoors, the second one is outdoors.
The students in the library look focused, while the ones in the park seem more relaxed.
Unlike the girl in the first picture, the boy is working with a partner.

words.ar: يخمّن / يتوقّع بناءً على ما يراه
words.ex: In this part of the exam, you need to speculate about the people in the photos.
Judging by her smile, she's just received some good news.
He looks relieved that the exam is finally over.
She seems frustrated because the experiment didn't work.
They must be exhausted after climbing all morning.
His facial expression suggests he's quite nervous.

dialogue.t: Look at this photo. How do you think the people are feeling, and what has just happened?
Well, they're a team of students holding a trophy, so they must have just won some kind of competition, maybe a robotics contest.
What about the boy on the left?
I'd imagine he's feeling quite relieved, judging by the way he's leaning back and closing his eyes. He might have been worried that their robot would break down.
And the girl at the back?
It looks as though she's trying to call someone, perhaps her parents, to tell them the news. She can't have expected to win, because she looks genuinely shocked.
What do you think might happen next?
They'll probably go out to celebrate, and I suppose their teacher might take a photo for the school website.

grammar.title: Past modals of deduction
grammar.ar: نستخدم must have + التصريف الثالث للفعل عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أن شيئًا حدث في الماضي، و might/may/could have عندما نظن أنه ربما حدث، و can't have عندما نكون متأكدين أنه لم يحدث. انتبه: لا نقول mustn't have للاستنتاج، بل can't have. هذه الأفعال ضرورية لوصف ما حدث للتو في الصور.
examples: She must have just finished a race because she's out of breath.
They might have lost their way, judging by the map in their hands.
He can't have slept well; he looks completely exhausted.

words.ex: Schools should encourage students to read for pleasure.
Graphic novels might appeal to teenagers who don't like long books.
I'm not sure I'd go along with the idea of making reading compulsory.
Prizes can be a good incentive for younger students.
Peer pressure can actually be positive if your friends love reading.
Setting up a book club would definitely be worthwhile.

dialogue.t: So, here are some ways to encourage teenagers to read more. Shall we start with book clubs? How do you feel about that idea?
I think it's quite effective, actually. Talking about books with friends makes reading feel more social, and it might appeal to people who usually find it boring.
True. What about giving prizes to students who read the most books?
I'm not sure I'd go along with that, because students might just choose very short books to win. The incentive should be enjoying the story, not the prize.
That's a fair point. Shall we move on to inviting authors to schools?
Yes, I love that one. Meeting a real writer can be really inspiring. How do you feel about it?
I agree, although it might be expensive for some schools.
Maybe they could organise online talks instead. That would still be worthwhile and much cheaper.

grammar.title: Prepositions + -ing form
grammar.ar: بعد حروف الجر مثل about و of و on و in نستخدم الفعل بصيغة ing- وليس المصدر مع to. يخطئ كثير من المتحدثين بالعربية فيقولون: How do you feel about to give، والصحيح How do you feel about giving. تذكّر أن صيغة ing- هنا تعمل كاسم، تمامًا مثل المصدر في العربية.
examples: How do you feel about inviting authors to school?
I'm not convinced of the benefits of giving prizes.
Shall we move on to talking about reading apps?

words.ex: Let's narrow it down to two options first.
After a long discussion, we finally settled on the library idea.
Maybe we can reach a compromise and combine both ideas.
Reading apps might be more effective in the long run.
I think the benefits clearly outweigh the costs.
Online author talks are a cost-effective solution.

dialogue.t: Now you have a minute to decide which of these ideas would be the most effective.
OK, so, we seem to agree that prizes aren't really the answer. Shall we narrow it down to book clubs and author visits?
Good idea. Personally, I'd choose author visits, because they're so memorable.
I can see your point, but I still think book clubs would be more effective in the long run. A visit only happens once, whereas a club meets every week.
That's true. And book clubs are probably more cost-effective too.
Exactly. The benefits definitely outweigh the effort of organising it.
Right, so which one shall we settle on?
If we had to choose just one, it would have to be the book club. Maybe as a compromise, the club could invite an author once a year.

grammar.title: Second conditional for hypothetical choices
grammar.ar: نستخدم الشرط الثاني (If + الماضي البسيط، would + الفعل) للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية، مثل الاختيار النهائي في المهمة التعاونية. العبارة it would have to be تعني أن هذا هو الخيار الوحيد المنطقي في رأيك. لا تضع would في جملة if، فنقول If we had وليس If we would have.
examples: If we had to choose just one, it would have to be the book club.
If the school had more money, author visits would be the best option.
If I were the head teacher, I'd set up a reading corner in every classroom.

words.ex: I suppose it depends on the student's personality.
Generally speaking, teenagers spend too much time online.
Not every family has access to fast internet.
Online learning can increase inequality between rich and poor students.
On the other hand, technology makes learning more flexible.
Sport and art are essential for a well-rounded education.

dialogue.t: Do you think all students should learn online in the future?
That's an interesting question. I suppose it depends on the age of the students. Older students can manage their time, whereas younger children need a teacher in the room.
Some people say exams put too much pressure on young people. What's your opinion?
Generally speaking, I'd agree, although in some cases a bit of pressure can actually push you to work harder. The problem is when exams are the only thing that matters.
Should schools teach practical skills like managing money?
I've never really thought about it, but now that you mention it, yes. A well-rounded education should prepare you for real life, not just for tests.
And does technology make education fairer?
Well, on the one hand, it gives people access to free resources. On the other hand, not everyone has a laptop, so it could increase inequality.

grammar.title: Depend on + noun / wh-clause
grammar.ar: بعد depend نستخدم دائمًا on وليس of أو from، وهو خطأ شائع لدى المتحدثين بالعربية بسبب الترجمة الحرفية. يمكن أن يأتي بعد depends on اسم، أو جملة تبدأ بكلمة استفهام مثل how و whether و what. هذه البنية مفيدة جدًا لإعطاء رأي متوازن وكسب الوقت للتفكير.
examples: I suppose it depends on the type of school.
It really depends on how much support students get at home.
Whether online learning works depends on what subject you're studying.

words.ex: She took a firm stance against banning phones at school.
In my opinion, the benefits of a phone ban outweigh the drawbacks.
Constant notifications are a huge distraction during lessons.
We shouldn't overlook the fact that some students need phones for medical reasons.
He made a compelling argument for keeping phones in lockers.
It's difficult for teachers to enforce a rule that students keep breaking.

dialogue.t: So, should smartphones be banned during the school day? What's your position?
I'd argue that they should be banned, because they're a constant distraction in class.
But lots of students use their phones for research and for staying in touch with their parents.
While it's true that phones can be useful, we shouldn't overlook the fact that most students use them for social media during lessons.
Couldn't schools just set clear rules instead of imposing a total ban?
The way I see it, the benefits of a ban outweigh the inconvenience. Students would concentrate better and actually talk to each other at break.
That's a strong stance. But what about emergencies?
Schools have landlines, and phones could be kept in lockers so students can reach them if something serious happens.

grammar.title: Concessive clauses with 'While'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'While' في بداية الجملة بمعنى 'مع أنّ' أو 'على الرغم من أنّ' لنعترف بفكرة الطرف الآخر قبل أن نقدّم رأينا الأقوى. يأتي بعد 'While' جملة كاملة (فاعل + فعل)، ثم فاصلة، ثم الجملة الرئيسية التي تحمل موقفنا. هذا الأسلوب يجعل حجتك تبدو متوازنة وأكثر إقناعاً. انتبه: لا نضيف 'but' بعد الفاصلة، فنقول: While it's true that..., we shouldn't... وليس While..., but we...
examples: While it's true that phones help with research, they also encourage cheating.
While some parents want constant contact, students need time to focus.
While I understand your concern, I still believe a ban is the best solution.

words.ex: I'll concede that online classes are more flexible.
Be ready to respond to your opponent's counterarguments.
That's a valid point, but it doesn't change my overall view.
Online learning offers flexibility for students who travel a lot.
Nothing can fully replace face-to-face interaction with a good teacher.
Studying from home requires a lot of self-discipline.

dialogue.t: I think online learning is the future. Students can study at their own pace.
Granted, online learning offers more flexibility, but most teenagers need a structured routine.
Online platforms can track your progress and give you instant feedback, though.
That's a fair point; however, feedback from a screen can't replace face-to-face interaction with a teacher.
Actually, many shy students feel more confident asking questions online.
Even if some students feel more comfortable online, it doesn't necessarily follow that they learn more effectively.
So you don't see any role for online learning at all?
I wouldn't go that far. It works well as a supplement, just not as a replacement for the classroom.

grammar.title: Conceding with 'Granted' and 'Even if'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'Granted, ..., but ...' لنعترف بأن نقطة الطرف الآخر صحيحة، ثم نعارضها مباشرة بـ 'but'. أما 'Even if' فتعني 'حتى لو'، وتُستخدم لنقول إن النتيجة لا تتغير حتى لو كانت الفكرة صحيحة. لا تخلط بين 'Even if' (حتى لو - افتراض) و'Even though' (مع أنّ - حقيقة مؤكدة). العبارة 'it doesn't necessarily follow that' تعني 'هذا لا يعني بالضرورة أن...' وهي طريقة قوية لكشف ضعف المنطق.
examples: Granted, online courses are cheaper, but they can feel isolating.
Even if online exams are convenient, it doesn't necessarily follow that they're fair.
That's a fair point; however, not every family has a reliable internet connection.

words.ex: Some European city centres have become completely car-free.
Banning cars would inevitably change the way people shop.
The city would need better infrastructure, such as shaded walkways.

words.ar: شخص يتنقّل يومياً (إلى العمل أو الدراسة)
words.ex: Thousands of commuters use the metro every morning.
Traffic congestion wastes hours of people's time every week.
How would elderly people cope with walking long distances?

dialogue.t: Imagine Riyadh became completely car-free. If the city were to ban cars, it would inevitably cut air pollution.
Maybe, but supposing cars disappeared tomorrow, how would people cope with walking in the summer heat?
The metro would carry most commuters. Had the city not invested in the Riyadh Metro, we might never have considered this idea at all.
True, but it doesn't reach every neighbourhood. If families were to lose their cars, it would inevitably make school runs much harder.
Not if they expanded bus routes and built air-conditioned stops.
Supposing that happened, how would shops and restaurants cope with deliveries?
They could use small electric vans at night, like some European cities do.
I'm still not convinced, but I'll admit the congestion would disappear overnight.

grammar.title: Hypotheticals: 'were to' and inverted 'Had'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'If + subject + were to + المصدر' للحديث عن موقف افتراضي في المستقبل يبدو بعيد الحدوث، وهي أكثر رسمية من 'If + الماضي البسيط'. أما 'Had + subject + past participle' فهي صيغة مقلوبة من الشرط الثالث تعني 'لو لم/لو أنّ ... في الماضي'، ونحذف فيها 'If'. مثلاً: Had they not built the metro = If they hadn't built the metro. هذه التراكيب تجعل أسلوبك في النقاش أكثر رقيّاً وإقناعاً.
examples: If the government were to ban cars, public transport would inevitably become overcrowded.
Had the city not built the metro, traffic would be even worse today.
Supposing petrol became very expensive, how would delivery companies cope?

words.ex: Regular exercise plays a big role in teenage wellbeing.
His claim is borne out by recent research.
A case in point is the school that added daily sport and saw grades improve.
Being part of a team can boost your self-esteem.
The findings suggest that active students sleep better.
Many teenagers say that running helps them manage anxiety before exams.

dialogue.t: Do you really think sport makes teenagers happier?
Definitely. According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression.
But that research might mainly be about adults.
Not really. This is borne out by studies of school students, which suggest that active teenagers tend to have higher self-esteem.
Statistics are one thing, but what about real life?
A case in point is my cousin. He joined a football team last year and he's far more confident now, which clearly shows that sport can change someone.
Couldn't that just be because he made new friends?
Partly, but that's exactly my point: team sport builds friendships, and friendships are a huge part of wellbeing.

grammar.title: Reporting evidence with passive structures
grammar.ar: في النقاش الجاد نستخدم المبني للمجهول لتقديم الأدلة بطريقة موضوعية، دون التركيز على الشخص. من التراكيب المفيدة: 'It has been shown that...' (ثبت أنّ...)، و'Studies are said to...'، و'This is borne out by...' (وهذا ما يؤكّده...). كما نستخدم 'According to + المصدر' لذكر مصدر المعلومة بوضوح. هذا يجعل ادعاءك يبدو مدعوماً بالحقائق لا مجرد رأي شخصي.
examples: It has been shown that teenagers who exercise regularly sleep better.
This is borne out by a survey of over a thousand students.
According to recent findings, team sports reduce feelings of loneliness.

words.ex: Sorry to cut in, but I think we're missing something important.
She held the floor until she had finished her argument.
A good moderator steers the conversation back to the main question.
We went off on a tangent and started talking about football.
Should volunteering be compulsory for secondary students?
You raised an interesting point about community service.

dialogue.t: I believe volunteering should be compulsory for all secondary students, because it teaches responsibility, and—
Sorry to cut in, but wouldn't forcing students defeat the whole purpose of volunteering?
If you'd just let me finish — even required volunteering exposes students to real problems in their community.
If I could just come back on what you said about responsibility, don't students learn that from part-time jobs too?
Possibly, but jobs are about money. Talking of money, some companies charge families a fortune for volunteering trips abroad...
Let's get back to the main issue, which is whether volunteering should be required at all.
Fair enough. My answer is yes, as long as students can choose the cause they support.
That's a compromise I could probably accept.

grammar.title: Softening interruptions with 'just' and 'could'
grammar.ar: عند مقاطعة شخص أو طلب الكلام في نقاش، نستخدم كلمات مخففة مثل 'just' و'could' و'if I may' حتى يبدو كلامنا مهذباً وليس عدوانياً. كلمة 'just' تقلل من حجم الطلب، و'If I could...' تجعله أشبه باستئذان. للاحتفاظ بالكلمة نقول مثلاً: 'If you'd just let me finish...' أو 'Let me just finish this point'. هذه العبارات مهمة جداً في المناقشات الجماعية واختبار المحادثة.
examples: If I could just add something here, volunteering also looks great on a CV.
Sorry to cut in, but could I just clarify what you mean by 'compulsory'?
Let me just finish this point, and then you can respond.

words.ex: On balance, I think homework does more good than harm.

words.ar: يتلخّص في / يرجع في جوهره إلى
words.ex: The whole debate boils down to how we use our time.

words.ar: بعد أخذ كل الأمور بعين الاعتبار
words.ex: All things considered, a shorter school day might be a good idea.
The main drawback of daily homework is the stress it causes.
Practice at home reinforces what students learn in class.
Too much homework can lead to burnout before exams.

dialogue.t: We've heard strong arguments on both sides. Would you like to give your closing statement?
Yes. Supporters of homework say it reinforces what we learn in class and builds discipline.
And what about the other side?
Opponents argue that too much homework leads to stress and burnout, and leaves no time for family or hobbies.
So where do you stand?
All things considered, homework does have value. On balance, I'm convinced that a small amount, focused on practice, is better than none at all.
Why not just get rid of it completely?
Because what it really boils down to is quality, not quantity. Twenty minutes of meaningful practice beats two hours of pointless busywork.

grammar.title: Emphasis with 'What' cleft sentences
grammar.ar: جملة 'What' المشطورة (cleft sentence) تُستخدم لإبراز الفكرة الأهم في نهاية الجملة، وهي مثالية للخاتمة الإقناعية. تركيبها: What + فاعل + فعل + is/was + الفكرة المهمة. مثلاً بدلاً من 'The debate boils down to quality' نقول: 'What it really boils down to is quality'. هذا الأسلوب يلفت انتباه المستمع ويجعل رسالتك الأخيرة قوية وواضحة.
examples: What really matters is how useful the homework is.
What I find most convincing is the evidence about stress levels.
What students need is time to rest as well as time to practise.

words.ex: Hegra was the first heritage site in Saudi Arabia to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
More than a hundred tombs were carved into the sandstone cliffs by the Nabataeans.
The view of the rock formations at sunset is absolutely breathtaking.
A surprising fact at the start can captivate your audience within seconds.
The Nabataeans were an ancient civilisation that controlled important trade routes.
How the tombs were built without modern tools still intrigues historians today.

dialogue.t: Can I try my opening on you? I want it to sound less like a textbook.
Sure, go ahead. I'll pretend I've never heard of AlUla.
Okay. Have you ever wondered why a desert valley in north-west Saudi Arabia attracts visitors from all over the world?
Nice, that question definitely makes me want to know the answer. What comes next?
Picture this: you're standing in front of a huge tomb carved into a golden cliff, and it's over two thousand years old.
That's really vivid. Maybe pause after 'picture this' so people have time to imagine it.
Good idea. Then I'll say: Today, I'd like to walk you through the history of Hegra, its Nabataean tombs and why it still matters to us.
Perfect. You've hooked me, and I know exactly what the talk will cover.

grammar.title: Rhetorical questions and imperatives for openings
grammar.ar: نستخدم السؤال البلاغي مثل Have you ever wondered why...? لإثارة فضول الجمهور دون انتظار إجابة حقيقية. لاحظ أن ترتيب الكلمات بعد why يكون ترتيب جملة خبرية وليس سؤالاً، فنقول why it attracts وليس why does it attract. ويُستخدم فعل الأمر مثل Picture this أو Imagine لدعوة المستمع إلى تخيّل مشهد ما. ثم نختم المقدمة بعبارة تحدد محتوى العرض مثل Today, I'd like to walk you through...
examples: Have you ever wondered why the Nabataeans chose such a remote place to build their tombs?
Picture this: the sun is rising over the sandstone cliffs and the whole valley is glowing orange.
Today, I'd like to walk you through three reasons why AlUla deserves its global reputation.

words.ex: Our school launched an initiative to clean up the local beach every month.
First, I'll briefly outline how the project started.
Could you elaborate on how you persuaded people to volunteer?
The tree-planting project is ongoing, and we hope to plant five hundred more trees.
One positive outcome was that neighbours started talking to each other more.
In terms of funding, the project relied entirely on local businesses.

dialogue.t: So far I've explained how our neighbourhood garden project started. Turning now to the challenges we faced, the biggest one was water.
That makes sense in our climate. How did you deal with it?
We installed a drip irrigation system, which cut our water use by almost half.
Impressive. Will you say more about that in the talk?
Yes. Let me elaborate on the irrigation system for a moment, because people always ask about it.
Good. And after the challenges, what's the final section?
This brings me to my next point, which is the impact on the community, especially on elderly residents who now meet there every evening.
Your transitions are really clear. I never felt lost between sections.

grammar.title: Signposting and non-defining relative clauses
grammar.ar: عبارات الربط مثل Turning now to... وThis brings me to my next point تساعد المستمع على معرفة الانتقال من قسم إلى آخر في العرض. بعد Turning now to نستخدم اسماً أو صيغة الفعل مع ing. وفي عبارة This brings me to my next point, which is... نستخدم جملة وصفية غير محددة تبدأ بـ which وتُفصل بفاصلة لإضافة معلومة توضيحية عن النقطة.
examples: Turning now to the results, we collected over two tonnes of rubbish in six months.
This brings me to my next point, which is how we kept volunteers motivated.
Let me elaborate on the role of local businesses for a moment.

words.ex: Saudi hospitality is famous among visitors from all over the world.
It's customary to stand up when an older person enters the room.
Serving the eldest guest first is a sign of respect.
Shaking the cup is a small gesture with a clear meaning.
Families usually break the fast with dates and water at sunset.
Eid is a time for large family gatherings and visits to relatives.

dialogue.t: In your last message you mentioned Arabic coffee. Is it just a drink, or is there more to it?
There's a lot more to it. It's customary to serve coffee with dates as soon as guests arrive.
Interesting. Does it matter who gets served first?
Yes, the host usually starts with the oldest or most important guest. Offering coffee is traditionally seen as a sign of generosity and respect.
And how do you say you don't want any more? In the UK we'd just say 'no thanks'.
Unlike in the UK, people here tend to gently shake the small cup from side to side. That tells the host you've had enough.
What a neat gesture! I'd never have guessed that.
And during Ramadan, it's customary to break the fast with dates and water before the main meal.

grammar.title: Describing customs: impersonal it and passive reporting
grammar.ar: نستخدم It's customary to + الفعل المجرد لوصف عادة اجتماعية بشكل عام دون تحديد فاعل. ونستخدم صيغة المبني للمجهول is seen as + اسم لنقل نظرة المجتمع إلى شيء ما، مثل is traditionally seen as a sign of. وللمقارنة بين ثقافتين نستخدم Unlike in + اسم البلد، ثم tend to + الفعل للتعبير عن سلوك شائع غالباً وليس دائماً.
examples: It's customary to remove your shoes when you enter someone's home.
Refusing food at a gathering is often seen as slightly impolite.
Unlike in many Western countries, people here tend to eat dinner quite late.

words.ex: She paused to build suspense before revealing what happened.
Once the sun set, the desert was pitch-black.
We were stranded for hours after our car got stuck in the sand.
To my relief, my phone still had a little battery left.
A truck appeared out of nowhere and stopped beside us.
Volunteering at the food bank was an unforgettable experience.

dialogue.t: You said your family camping trip didn't go to plan. What happened?
We'd been driving through the desert for about three hours when suddenly the car sank into soft sand.
Oh no! Were you completely stranded?
Pretty much. No sooner had my dad started digging than the sun went down and everything turned pitch-black.
That sounds terrifying. How did you get out?
A truck appeared out of nowhere. To our relief, the driver was a local guide and he pulled us out in minutes.
What a story! Did it put you off camping?
Not at all. Looking back, I realise that it was the most unforgettable trip we've ever had.

grammar.title: Past perfect continuous and inversion with No sooner
grammar.ar: نستخدم الماضي التام المستمر had been + فعل ing لوصف حدث استمر فترة في الماضي قبل أن يقاطعه حدث مفاجئ بالماضي البسيط. أما No sooner had + فاعل + التصريف الثالث + than فتعني ما إن حدث كذا حتى حدث كذا، وتُستخدم لإضافة التشويق. لاحظ أن الفعل المساعد had يأتي قبل الفاعل بعد No sooner وهذا يسمى القلب.
examples: I'd been waiting at the airport for two hours when suddenly my name was announced.
No sooner had we arrived at the farm than it started pouring with rain.
Looking back, I realise that helping others taught me more than any lesson at school.

words.ex: My grandfather loves to reminisce about his childhood in old Jeddah.
Neighbourhoods used to be very close-knit, and everyone knew each other.
Back in the day, there were no shopping malls in our city.
New roads and buildings have completely transformed Riyadh.
She pointed out that families used to share meals with their neighbours.

words.ar: على ما يبدو / حسب ما يُقال
words.ex: Apparently, my grandmother walked to school every day.

dialogue.t: Did you manage to interview your grandmother for the project?
Yes, and she had so much to say. She told me that our street had been just sand when she first moved there.
Really? It's full of shops and traffic now.
I know. She pointed out that families used to leave their doors open all day because everyone trusted each other.
That sounds like a very close-knit community. What about entertainment?
Apparently, back then, people would gather on rooftops in the evening to escape the heat and chat.
Did she say whether she prefers life now or then?
She said she missed the old closeness, but she admitted that life was much easier today.

grammar.title: Reported speech: backshifting, used to and would
grammar.ar: عند نقل كلام شخص بأفعال مثل told me that أو pointed out that نرجع زمن الفعل خطوة إلى الماضي غالباً، فيصبح الماضي البسيط ماضياً تاماً had + التصريف الثالث. أما used to فلا تتغير في الكلام المنقول. ونستخدم would + الفعل المجرد للحديث عن عادات متكررة في الماضي، لكن ليس عن الحالات الدائمة مثل live أو be.
examples: He told me that he had worked as a fisherman before the port was built.
She pointed out that children used to play in the street until sunset.
Apparently, back then, people would visit each other without calling first.

words.ex: Could you clarify what you meant by sustainable tourism?
Let me rephrase that, because I don't think I explained it clearly.

words.w: off the top of my head
words.ar: دون الرجوع إلى مصدر / من الذاكرة مباشرة
words.ex: Off the top of my head, I'd say about a million people visit each year.
I can only give you a rough estimate of the cost.
That's an interesting point, and I'll look into it after the session.
You raise a valid point about the impact of tourism on the environment.

dialogue.t: Thanks for the presentation. How many tourists actually visited AlUla last year?
That's a great question; it's something many people ask. I'm afraid I don't have the exact figures, but numbers have risen sharply in recent years.
Okay. You also mentioned protecting the tombs. Doesn't more tourism damage them?
That's a valid point. Visitors can only enter Hegra on guided tours, so access is carefully controlled.
Sorry, I'm not sure I follow. Why does that make a difference?
To put it another way, guides make sure people don't touch the carvings or climb on the tombs.
Ah, that's clearer now. Do you know if there are plans to limit visitor numbers?
Honestly, I'm not certain, but I'll look into it and share what I find with the class.

grammar.title: Polite hedging and rephrasing
grammar.ar: عند عدم معرفة الإجابة نستخدم عبارات مهذبة تخفف من حدة الرد مثل I'm afraid I don't have... ثم نضيف but لتقديم معلومة بديلة مفيدة. ونستخدم To put it another way أو In other words لإعادة شرح فكرة بكلمات أبسط عندما لا يفهمها السائل. كما تمنحنا عبارة That's a great question وقتاً قصيراً للتفكير قبل الإجابة.
examples: I'm afraid I don't have the exact figures, but I can give you a rough estimate.
To put it another way, the project saves money and protects the environment at the same time.
That's a great question; I hadn't actually thought about it from that angle.
